papers.title: Region-Specific Changes in the Aging Enteric Nervous System
papers.abstract: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

papers.title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
papers.abstract: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.

papers.title: Modern speech recognition systems exhibit human-like word recognition but superhuman use of statistical dependencies between words
papers.abstract: Advances in machine learning have yielded machine systems that approach human performance on real-world perception tasks. For speech recognition, it remains unclear whether such models' behavior resembles that of humans. We addressed this question by measuring word recognition abilities in humans and models across 272 speech distortions, providing a detailed behavioral fingerprint. Three recent industry speech recognition models trained on hundreds of years of speech outperformed humans. However, in conditions where linguistic context was removed, they matched human performance well, suggesting that the models are superhuman in their ability to leverage statistical dependencies between words. Experiments manipulating model training data suggest that training data variability and realism contribute to the match to human perception. Overall, the results show that superhuman performance is now possible with systems that are optimized over enough data and suggest that accurate models of human speech recognition require optimization over appropriate tasks and amounts of speech.

papers.title: Cask dysfunction in inhibitory neurons reveals distinct synaptic and epileptic phenotypes in mouse models of CASK-related disorder
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a major neurological manifestation of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, yet how genetic disruptions produce distinct seizure phenotypes remains poorly understood. CASK-related disorder is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder frequently accompanied by epilepsy. It is caused by pathogenic variants in CASK, which encodes calcium/calmodulin-dependent serine protein kinase, a protein with diverse molecular functions. Here, we establish sex-specific mouse models of CASK-related disorder and identify epileptic phenotypes in both sexes. Cell type-specific Cask deletion identifies inhibitory neurons as a critical cellular locus of distinct forms of epileptic activity. Cask deficiency in parvalbumin- or somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons primarily causes spike-wave discharges or motor seizures, accompanied by reduced spontaneous or evoked inhibitory synaptic transmission, respectively. Thus, Cask dysfunction in different inhibitory synapses and circuits produces distinct seizure phenotypes. These findings reveal how cell type-specific synaptic dysfunction shapes epilepsy in CASK-related disorder and may provide insights into diverse neurological phenotypes of neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: Molecular analysis of 55 dopamine transporter variants from psychiatric patients reveals convergent mechanisms of dysfunction
papers.abstract: Rare genetic variants are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuropsychiatric disease and may reveal underlying pathobiological mechanisms. The dopamine transporter (DAT), encoded by SLC6A3, regulates dopaminergic neurotransmission through rapid dopamine (DA) reuptake. Although disease-associated DAT variants have been linked to disorders ranging from infantile parkinsonism to neuropsychiatric disease, the molecular basis of DAT dysfunction remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigated 55 DAT missense variants identified in the iPSYCH2012-nested case-control cohort. By assessing transport activity, inhibitor binding, cell-surface expression, subcellular localization, amphetamine responsiveness and constitutive DA efflux, we resolved the variants into seven phenotypic classes. These reflected distinct molecular defects, including impaired substrate and ion coupling, destabilized intramolecular interactions, and defective folding, trafficking or surface expression. Molecular dynamics simulations provided structural insight into representative variants. Collectively, our findings reveal mechanistic convergence of genetically diverse DAT variants and establish a framework for interpreting the pathogenicity of newly identified SLC6A3 variants.

papers.title: Thrombin cleavage of circulating osteopontin in the lung drives hippocampal neuroinflammation and acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction after acute kidney injury
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical problem with high morbidity and mortality due to frequently occurring secondary organ complications, including acute neurologic dysfunction, such as delirium. Specific mechanisms responsible for this kidney-brain crosstalk are unknown but hypothesized to include uremic toxins and neuroinflammation secondary to systemic inflammation. Here we show that uremic mice with AKI show hippocampal monocytic neuroinflammation associated with acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction only in the presence of circulating osteopontin fragments. Mechanistically, circulating osteopontin (OPN/Spp1) released by the injured kidney was cleaved by thrombin in the lung into OPN-N and OPN-C-terminal fragments. Both OPN fragments were required to drive upregulation of the monocyte chemoattractant chemokine-ligand-2 (CCL2) in hippocampal endothelial cells. AKI mice lacking OPN or unable to activate OPN by thrombin cleavage showed kidney injury and serum uremic toxin elevations like wt controls but were protected from hippocampal CCL2 upregulation, monocyte recruitment, and delirium-like symptoms. Systemic application of an OPN or CCL2 neutralizing antibody was protective. Our results suggest that a specific kidney-released circulating factor, osteopontin, drives acute neurologic dysfunction after AKI and challenge the widely held hypothesis that uremic toxins play a dominant role. They also identify thrombin cleavage of OPN as a potential therapeutic target and critical switch for the remote functions of circulating OPN.

papers.title: Aging remodels the neuronal activity-dependent transcriptome
papers.abstract: Experience-driven neuronal activity induces coordinated transcriptional programs in neurons and glia that support plasticity and memory. How aging reshapes these activity-regulated gene (ARG) programs, and whether activity mitigates or exacerbates aging phenotypes, remain open questions with implications for cognitive decline. Here, we develop novel-environment and chemogenetic paradigms to characterize age-dependent remodeling of ARG transcriptomes in the mouse hippocampus at single-cell resolution. Aging contracts youthful ARG programs in both gene number and dynamic range, a contraction that persists under controlled chemogenetic stimulation independent of behavior. In parallel, novel experience in older mice reveals a latent transcriptional competence. First, distinct sets of genes respond to neuronal activity selectively in older cells. Second, enhancing activity in older animals partially reverses, or buffers, basal aging-associated changes across the transcriptome. Novel experience counteracts aging-associated changes in the target genes of the memory regulator CREB1 and the ER-stress sensor ATF6 across cell types. These data constitute a resource for neuronal activity-dependent transcription across the lifespan and identify a basis for the benefits of cognitive engagement: novel experience buffers age-related transcriptional drift.

papers.title: Counterfactual aging in individual digital twin brains uncovers a latent dimension of resilience to aging
papers.abstract: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93-0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal-angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.

papers.title: PROGMF: Progressive Multimodal Fusion and Representation Learning for Incomplete Neuroimaging Data
papers.abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging studies often involve cohorts with partially overlapping data modalities. Many conventional multimodal fusion methods rely on participants with complete observations across the selected modalities. We introduce Progressive Multimodal Fusion (ProgMF), a novel fusion framework for learning multimodal source representations from incomplete neuroimaging data without imputing missing observations. ProgMF integrates modalities sequentially through independent vector analysis (IVA), cross-stage component alignment, and anchor-guided representation transfer, allowing information learned from earlier-stage cohorts to inform subsequent multimodal decompositions. We evaluated ProgMF on four neuroimaging-inspired synthetic modalities, while varying subject overlap, observation noise, modality relatedness, and fusion orders. ProgMF generally achieved lower source-recovery errors than complete-case IVA and the evaluated imputation-based methods, with larger improvements as multimodal subject overlap decreased. We further applied ProgMF to structural MRI gray matter, resting-state functional network connectivity, and 18F-florbetapir (AV45) amyloid positron emission tomography data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. ProgMF achieved higher mean cross-modal fusion scores than the imputation-based baselines and a modest improvement over complete-case IVA. Among the 293 participants with complete multimodal observations, two recovered source component vectors showed significant associations with clinical diagnosis across cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia groups. Both sources were also significantly associated with cognitive performance and dementia severity. The recovered sources exhibited diagnosis-related structural and amyloid PET patterns involving regions such as the hippocampi, precuneus, and cingulate cortices. Our findings support progressive representation transfer as an effective approach for recovering coherent, interpretable multimodal sources from participants with incomplete modality coverage.

papers.title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise
papers.abstract: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.

papers.title: Oligodendrocyte Development and Myelination in the 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
papers.abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, including a 25% chance of developing schizophrenia (SCZ). SCZ is prevalent in 0.4-0.7% of the population. Evidence suggests that the cognitive deficits of SCZ may be caused by neurodevelopmental disconnection due to impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) maturation and myelination. We hypothesized that the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome impairs OL life cycle progression, halting oligodendrocytes in their immature phase and preventing advancement to the mature stage. This in turn creates myelination changes, demonstrated by a decrease in myelin. To test this, we utilized a 22q11.2 deletion mouse model focusing on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a late-myelinating brain region. We evaluated PFC regions (mPFC, dlPFC, mOFC, lOFC) in adolescent (P14 and P28) mutant mice and controls. Additionally, we examined the two-hit hypothesis of schizophrenia using a maternal separation model. At P28, mutant mice displayed a significant increase in immature OLs and mature OLs in the PFC, and a decrease in myelination and myelin process length compared to controls. At P14, mutant mice showed subtle reductions in oligodendrocyte precursor cells and subtle myelination alterations in the mPFC. When considering the two-hit hypothesis, we saw equivalent reductions in myelination in the genetic-only, environmental-only, and two-hit groups. Together, these data demonstrate that the 22q11.2 deletion impairs OL maturation and functional myelination between P14 to P28, a critical window for neurodevelopment. Examining the impact of SCZ on OLs could reveal key intervention targets before SCZ symptom onset, and may determine the role of OLs and the 22q11.2 deletion in neural disconnectivity in schizophrenia.

papers.title: Neuronal activity regulates glycolysis to sculpt synaptic transmission
papers.abstract: Neuronal computation imposes rapid, localized changes in energy consumption, yet how energy production is regulated at such fine spatiotemporal scales is incompletely understood. Using two photon imaging of neuronal activity and energy metabolism in Drosophila , we show that neurons recruit glycolysis in less than a second, with cell-type and subcellular specificity. This coupling scales with neuronal activity and is regulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Activity-induced glycolysis is tightly correlated with presynaptic sites in cholinergic neurons, and is required for cholinergic but not glutamatergic neurotransmission. In cholinergic neurons, glycolysis supports both energetic demand and acetylcholine biosynthesis, with ATP citrate lyase linking these functions by both activating acetylcholine biosynthesis and disinhibiting glycolytic flux. These findings establish glycolysis as a previously unrecognized regulator of cell-type specific computation.

papers.title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
papers.abstract: Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. We studied 101 youths aged 8-18 years using brain entropy (BEN), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Voxelwise and seven-network models evaluated age associations and task-by-age interactions while adjusting for sex, head motion, and gray-matter anatomy. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF-AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain-behavior coupling.

papers.title: Spectral and complexity-based signatures of advanced concentration absorption meditation: A high-density EEG study of jhana
papers.abstract: Advanced meditation provides structured and reproducible alterations of consciousness that are increasingly used as model states for the neuroscience of consciousness. Jhana-type advanced concentration absorption meditation (ACAM-J) consists of eight progressively deepening absorption states (ACAM-J1-8) in which sensory and self-referential content gradually attenuate. We applied high-density EEG and a comprehensive multidimensional battery of spectral and complexity measures to characterize each ACAM-J state individually in 20 advanced meditators, together with phenomenological ratings. ACAM-J produced widespread posterior-central reductions in oscillatory and aperiodic power, posterior aperiodic flattening across all eight states, and convergent increases in entropy-based complexity over the posterior cortex, with power effects strengthening with phenomenological depth. Crucially, neural complexity remained elevated even in the late, most minimal and unified states, in opposition to the prevailing account that links higher neural entropy to richer phenomenal content. Between practitioners, lower power and higher entropy accompanied more visual and auditory but less bodily content, a redistribution rather than an enrichment of experience; within practitioners, only reduced low-frequency power tracked wider attention and less narrative thought. ACAM-J thus emerges as a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of the spectrum of altered consciousness, and reveals a previously unquantified dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness for specific ACAM-J states.

papers.title: Stability and flexibility in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task emerge from goal-directed inference and planning under the free-energy principle
papers.abstract: In goal-directed behavior, the brain has to balance stability and flexibility. Stability means keeping the current recognition of environmental context, whereas flexibility means switching to a new one. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (WCST) is a standard task for studying this balance. In this task, stability is keeping the category estimate after correct feedback, and flexibility is switching it after incorrect feedback. Computational models have been proposed to elucidate the mechanism behind this balance. However, most models are given a variable for each category in advance, and every model treats correct feedback as desirable from the start. These models cover neither the category learning process nor the goal-directed process that adjusts the card selection to get correct feedback. To explain both processes under one principle, we modeled the WCST with a hierarchical recurrent neural network based on the Free Energy Principle (FEP). The model first infers the environment from observations and then plans the card selection to reach the goal. In both steps, the model minimizes prediction error based on the FEP. For inference, the error lies between the predicted signals and the received signals. For planning, it lies between the predicted feedback and the correct feedback. As a result, the latent states formed category-related clusters during learning. In the testing phase, the model kept the estimate after correct feedback and switched it after incorrect feedback. Removing the goal-directed process degraded the keeping and the switching. This implies that the two processes and this balance emerge from the FEP.

papers.title: Timing and meaning in spoken thought relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics
papers.abstract: When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing ({beta} = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.

papers.title: Heterogeneous short-term plasticity reformats latent temporal information into an explicit population clock
papers.abstract: Short-term plasticity (STP) supports diverse synaptic-level computations, but how its organization across a circuit shapes emergent, network-level dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we first characterize STP across sparse inputs to Kenyon cells in the Drosophila mushroom body, revealing an unstructured and near-random organization that could not be explained by either pre- or postsynaptic cell identity. Rather than representing biological noise, an experimentally constrained network model instead shows how this heterogeneous organization reformats temporal information embedded in presynaptic spike rate trajectories into a behaviorally relevant population clock. Although an ideal observer could recover the same degree of temporal information from most alternative models, only the STP-mediated transformation made that information accessible to a biologically realistic decoder. Together, our results identify heterogeneous STP as a distributed biophysical mechanism that collectively functions as a temporal basis set to support circuit computations across variable input statistics.

papers.title: Children become accurate years before they become fast: electroencephalography dates the separate maturation of decision components
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions, a hallmark of cognitive development, become faster and more accurate from early childhood to adulthood, but whether the underlying components mature together, as a single global gain in processing speed would predict, or on separate timetables remains unclear. Behaviour alone cannot distinguish whether age-related improvement reflects clearer sensory encoding, more efficient evidence accumulation, fewer attention lapses or shorter non-decision processes, and prior direct measurements have typically come from small samples spanning limited age ranges. We analysed electroencephalography from 1,534 participants aged 5 to 21 years in the Healthy Brain Network during a contrast-change discrimination task. On the same trials, we measured the visual response and an evidence-accumulation signal, while a decision model estimated accumulation efficiency, attention lapses and non-decision time. We found that the visual response did not grow with age and retained 77% of its strength on missed targets. Instead, accuracy improved through fewer lapses and more efficient accumulation, both reaching half of their developmental change by about 9 years, whereas speed improved later: non-decision time shortened between 11 and 14 years and was longer in children whose accumulation signal rose later. These findings show that perceptual decision-making matures through dissociable stages rather than a single global increase in processing speed: mechanisms supporting accuracy mature in middle childhood, whereas those supporting the fastest responses continue to develop into early adolescence. This framework links developmental theories of processing speed to neural mechanisms of decision-making and provides a reference for identifying which component is disrupted in children who struggle.

papers.title: False-negative assessment of NanoNewron's NewroBus blood-brain barrier delivery platform in the JAX apical-domain-humanized TfR1 mouse
papers.abstract: Humanized transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) mice are frequently used to evaluate blood-brain barrier (BBB) delivery, yet available strains differ in the extent and design of receptor humanization. We compared two NanoNewron NewroBus-based anti-TNF constructs, NN-841 (D3 TfR1-binding module) and NN-843 (A2 module), in JAX #038212 (humanized apical domain), Cyagen C001584 (human extracellular-domain CDS model), Cyagen C001860 (human extracellular-domain genomic replacement model), and wild-type controls. Thirty mice received intravenous injections and were evaluated 24 h later. Brain parenchymal-fraction signals were reported in all 12 Cyagen mice, but in none of six JAX or 12 wild-type animals. Serum concentrations were measurable in every group and followed the same rank order for both constructs: Cyagen-CDS>Cyagen-HU>wild type >JAX. Mean CDS-to-JAX serum ratios were approximately 13--fold for both constructs. Compared with the Cyagen-HU strain, the CDS strain showed higher parenchymal concentrations; the ratio of mean parenchymal to mean serum concentration increased prominently for NN-841, but only modestly for NN-843. These findings indicate that model choice influences 24-h circulating concentrations and apparent BBB delivery. Circulating soluble human TfR1-mediated stabilization and endothelial TfR1-dependent transport are plausible, untested explanations for strain-dependent differences. A negative brain-delivery result in JAX #038212 alone cannot be taken as evidence that NewroBus lacks BBB delivery activity

papers.title: Robustness of cortical distortion metrics to unmodelled OPM errors
papers.abstract: The estimate of cortical current flow from magnetic fields measured outside the head is an ill-posed problem. Recent work using head casts to minimise co-registration errors in conventional cryogenic magnetoencephalography (MEG) has shown that ground truth anatomy can be used to judge between different inversion schemes and metrics. Inversion algorithms or metrics that are insensitive to anatomical distortion are unlikely to reflect correct assumptions about the underlying current distribution. Here we aim to identify constraints when using this approach to validate current flow estimated from recordings made with optically pumped MEG (OP-MEG). To do so, we used simulations contaminated by different sources of (typically unmodelled) error. For example: error in the estimate of the true sensor positions or orientations and the effects of unmodelled gain changes. In accordance with previous work, with no unmodelled errors, distortion was minimized when the simulation and the inversion assumptions matched. We then quantified the amount of error (in mm) relative to the true cortical mesh that one might expect in empirical recordings (given gain, position and orientation errors). We found that the approach was tolerant to independent sensor position errors of less than 2 mm (per axis); orientation errors of less than 5 degrees; fixed array displacements of less than 10 degrees and to random sensor gain errors of less than 10%. Additionally, we tested this approach using two empirical OPM datasets. We found that source reconstructions based on both minimum norm and beamformer assumptions were sensitive to the underlying anatomy.

papers.title: TDP2 couples PKA-CREB signalling to genome stability in human cerebellar development
papers.abstract: Transcription and neuronal activity in the central nervous system generate abundant DNA damage, particularly DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), rendering neural cells - and cerebellar neurons especially - vulnerable to genome instability. Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2, also known as TTRAP) resolves topoisomerase-2-linked DSBs, and biallelic TDP2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 23 (SCAR23), yet how DNA repair shapes human cerebellar development is unknown. Here we model SCAR23 in cerebellar organoids derived from patient induced pluripotent stem cells carrying TDP2 c.650del and from prime-edited isogenic TDP2 c.400C>T lines. TDP2 inactivation caused organoid hypoplasia during FGF8b-dependent cerebellar specification, which was reversed by TDP2 complementation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics across three developmental stages revealed early dysregulation of ribosome biogenesis, attenuated CREB1 regulon activity and a subsequent failure of Purkinje cell maturation. TDP2 inactivation upregulated PKIB, a cerebellum-enriched inhibitor of protein kinase A, lowering PKA and CREB phosphorylation. Whole-genome sequencing showed excess de novo deletions in mutant organoids, enriched at candidate cis-regulatory elements of neurodevelopmental genes. Pharmacological activation of the cAMP-PKA cascade restored CREB phosphorylation, reduced DNA damage and rescued organoid growth. These findings link developmental signalling to genome maintenance in the human cerebellum and identify the cAMP-PKA-CREB axis as a candidate therapeutic target in DNA-repair-deficient cerebellar disease.

papers.title: Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridging Network for Motor Execution to Motor Imagery EEG Transfer in Brain-Computer Interfaces
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) hold promising application prospects in the fields of limb motor rehabilitation and human-computer interaction. However, the reliability of MI calibration data is limited by the difficulty of verifying participants' engagement during motor imagerywhereas motor execution (ME) provides a more readily supervised source of motor-related information.To investigate the potential of ME-derived knowledge for assisting MI decoding, we propose a Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridge Network (SE-RTBNet) to achieve accurate intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer from ME to MI. The proposed framework consists of two major components: a shared encoder and a residual task-bridge module. The shared encoder extracts stable general motor representations from multi-band EEG signals and explores the shared feature patterns underlying ME and MI tasks. The residual task-bridge module is equipped with a performance-aware routing mechanism. It adaptively compensates for task-specific discrepancies between the two tasks, enabling precise cross-task feature alignment and knowledge transfer. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, experiments are conducted on three public datasets. The proposed method achieves average classification accuracies of 69.39%, 74.61%, and 98.94%, respectively, and outperforms existing transfer-learning algorithms in overall performance. Our model provides an effective strategy for reducing dependence on extensive MI calibration data through intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer.The source code of the proposed SE-RTBNet is publicly available at https://github.com/Daisyzyx2002/SE-RTBNet

papers.title: Two co-occurring dynamics explain the organization of a natural movement repertoire
papers.abstract: Natural movements vary across multiple kinematic features, making it difficult to identify the dynamics shared across movements that generate a behavioral repertoire. Here, we provide a low-dimensional, interpretable generative account of the larval zebrafish hunting repertoire that links tail dynamics to behavioral outcomes. Analysis of thousands of movements spanning classically defined bout types revealed that repertoire diversity arises from continuous combinations of two simultaneously expressed dynamics: a slow, non-oscillatory bending component and a fast, oscillatory undulatory component. An analytical model captured these dynamics with six interpretable parameters and accurately reconstructed movements across the full repertoire and at two developmental stages. Different parameters predicted distinct aspects of movement outcome: maximum tail bend predicted change in heading angle, maximum tail curvature and movement duration predicted distance traveled, and oscillatory asymmetry predicted displacement direction. Relationships among the dynamical parameters constrained the movements and outcomes available to the animal. Key parameters could also be recovered directly from empirical tail kinematics, establishing them as experimentally accessible movement variables rather than model-dependent latent dimensions. Together, these results explain both the diversity and limits of a natural movement repertoire through constrained combinations of co-occurring dynamics.

papers.title: Modeling CNS inflammatory demyelination using myelin-directed CAR T cells
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis therapies remain confined to immunomodulatory agents that reduce inflammatory activity; none restores lost myelin, and disability can continue to accumulate independently of relapses. Development of remyelinating therapies has been hindered by models that incompletely reproduce the persistently inflamed lesions in which remyelination fails. Here we show that chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells targeting myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) build such lesions on demand. Human CD4+ CAR T cells transferred into immunodeficient mice infiltrated the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerve, producing perivascular demyelinating lesions, with reproducible optic nerve involvement. Within these discrete optic nerve lesions, treatment with the remyelinating compound clemastine reduced lesion size and improved optic nerve conduction, despite persistent inflammation. Thus, this MOG CAR T model reproduces key features of inflammatory demyelinating disease and enables testing of remyelinating therapies; more broadly, it introduces CAR T cells as programmable perturbative agents for building defined pathology in vivo.

papers.title: Biological Embedding of Social Experience Over Genomic and Neural Time Scales
papers.abstract: The "Neurons for Today, Genes for Tomorrow model" (NTGT) predicts how the brain's neural and molecular control systems interact to regulate biological embedding, whereby social experience alters the brain to shape future behavior. We report here on the first test of this model, using honey bee queen retinue pheromone (QRP) and behavioral, single-nucleus transcriptomic, and electrophysiological analyses. Consistent with theory, weaker exposure triggered a simple attraction response and transcriptomic changes primarily in the antennal lobes (AL), whereas stronger exposure induced transcriptomic changes in the mushroom bodies, a brain region affecting more complex behavior. In addition, AL electrophysiological responses to QRP were enhanced after stronger exposure, also consistent with theory. We also showed how individual differences in biological embedding can be explained by NTGT, with individual differences in brain gene regulatory network topology, especially in specific sensory cell clusters, supporting a new mechanistic framework for behavioral regulation.

papers.title: Stage-Dependent Requirement for SETX in Human Motor Neuron Maturation and Survival
papers.abstract: Senataxin (SETX) is an RNA/DNA helicase involved in transcription, RNA processing, R-loop resolution, and genome maintenance. Mutations in SETX cause neurological disorders, but its role in human motor neuron (MN) development remains unclear. Here, we examined SETX function using isogenic SETX knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), shRNA-mediated knockdown, and direct conversion of fibroblasts into MNs. SETX expression increased during differentiation from hiPSCs to neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and MNs. SETX loss slowed hiPSC and NPC proliferation without preventing MN generation. However, SETX-deficient MNs developed shorter neurites, dystrophic swellings, and progressive neuronal loss. MEA recordings showed reduced firing and burst activity and almost no synchronized network bursts. RNA hybrid accumulation increased after SETX loss, with the largest relative increase in MNs among the cell types examined. RNA-seq revealed altered neurodevelopmental gene expression at the NPC stage and during MN differentiation, together with increased expression of stress- and apoptosis-associated genes. Proteomic analysis identified changes in proteins involved in neuronal structure, synaptic function, RNA regulation, and cellular homeostasis. Concordant decreases in selected RNAs and proteins supported disruption of neuronal structural and synaptic programs. Together, these findings reveal a stage-dependent requirement for SETX and identify SETX as an important regulator of transcriptional programs governing human MN maturation, function, and survival, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the selective MN vulnerability associated with SETX-linked neurological diseases.

papers.title: Multistage gradient-based whole-cortex modeling for joint inference of regional circuit heterogeneity and interregional structural connectivity
papers.abstract: Current non-invasive neuroimaging methods cannot directly resolve regional circuit heterogeneity and interregional structural connectivity, limiting mechanistic understanding of brain structure-function relationships and accurate whole-brain modeling. Here we introduce StaGIC (Staged Gradient-based Inference of Circuitry), a method that jointly infers regional circuit heterogeneity and model-constrained structural connectivity (SC) from resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and functional connectivity dynamics (FCD). Ablation and synthetic-recovery experiments show that staged optimization improves fits to functional data and ground-truth parameter recovery, with inferred SC remaining highly consistent across retained solutions from independent optimization runs. In human data, freely optimized regional parameters exhibit consistent relationships with cortical hierarchy across parcellations, while SC inference substantially improves FC reconstruction. In macaque and marmoset data, inferred SC shows stronger correlation with tracer-derived projections than diffusion MRI estimates, particularly for long-range connections. As a proof of concept in computational psychiatry, group-level models of major depressive disorder (MDD) reproduce MDD-associated FC differences and generate exploratory hypotheses about hierarchical differentiation and interregional projection organization. StaGIC thus provides a differentiable framework for inferring multiscale cortical organization from non-invasive functional imaging.

papers.title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
papers.abstract: Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

papers.title: Optoretinographic measurements of cone photoreceptor function in disease-affected retinas
papers.abstract: Optoretinography (ORG) provides a noninvasive approach for measuring stimulus-evoked photoreceptor responses in the living human retina, but its application to retinal disease using clinically translatable imaging systems remains limited. Here, we applied velocity-based ORG using a clinical-grade swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT) system to assess photoreceptor function in disease-affected human retinas and healthy controls. Following pupil dilation and dark adaptation, repeated B-scans were acquired at 400 Hz during visible-light stimulation using a phase-sensitive 100-kHz, 1060-nm swept-source OCT system. Stimulus-evoked optical path length changes between the inner segment/outer segment junction (IS/OS) and cone outer segment tips (COST) were used to quantify cone outer-segment responses. Healthy retinas exhibited rapid and reproducible responses characterized by an initial outer-segment contraction followed by elongation, whereas disease-affected retinas exhibited quantitatively reduced or altered response amplitudes and temporal dynamics. ORG also detected functional improvement following treatment in a vitamin-A-deficient retina. These findings demonstrate the ability of velocity-based ORG to quantitatively detect photoreceptor dysfunction and functional change using a clinically compatible OCT platform, supporting its potential as a noninvasive functional biomarker for retinal disease and therapeutic response.

papers.title: Probe-assisted Structural Topography Reveals In-tissue Lesion Heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Disease lesions are typically defined by morphology, yet this classification often masks underlying structural heterogeneity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) plaques appear as featureless deposits under conventional microscopy, obscuring distinct sub-regions with divergent packing, maturation, and pathological potential. Here, we present Probe-Assisted Structural Topography of Amyloid (PASTA), a single-staining framework that combines a novel pan-A{beta} probe (NapIM) with fluorescence lifetime-resolved detection and super-resolution microscopy to unmask this hidden complexity. Leveraging PASTA, we quantify plaque maturity via the Protofibril Index (PFI) at sub-lesion level, and resolve the three-dimensional (3D) in-tissue architecture of A{beta} plaques at ~30 nm resolution, identifying radially extended A{beta} branches as fundamental structural units. PASTA enables structural mapping across plaque developmental stages to reconstruct their dynamic growth trajectories, resolving two distinct assembly lineages (dense and loose) with divergent growth paths that converge to a mixed terminal subtype and share a common transition point. We further applied PASTA for mapping microglial engagement, linking interdigitated microglial contacts to dense plaque compaction and uncontacted fibril branches to loose morphology. Together, PASTA provides an unprecedented framework for understanding A{beta} heterogeneity, nanoscale architecture, and microglial-mediated remodeling in AD.
